# Testing

DASCore's test suite is run with [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/). While in the base dascore repo
(and after [installing DASCore for development](dev_install.qmd)) invoke pytest from the command line:

<!--pytest-codeblocks:skip-->
```bash
pytest tests
```

You can also use the cov flags to check coverage. Please make sure you don't
introduce large blocks of dead code.

<!--pytest-codeblocks:skip-->
```bash
pytest tests --cov dascore --cov-report term-missing
```

If you would like to test the IO modules it can be done like so:

<!--pytest-codeblocks:skip-->
```bash
pytest tests/test_io
```

Or a particular IO module:

<!--pytest-codeblocks:skip-->
```bash
pytest tests/test_io/test_dasdae.py
```

Pytest is highly configurable and has some rather useful flags such as
-s, -x, and --pdb (especially with [pdbpp](https://github.com/pdbpp/pdbpp)).


To run the docstring tests use the following:

<!--pytest-codeblocks:skip-->
```bash
pytest dascore --doctest-modules
```

To validate executable examples in the hand-written documentation without building the full site, generate the mirrored tests with:

```bash
python scripts/generate_doc_code_tests.py
```

Then run the generated tests:

```bash
pytest tests/test_autogenerated_doccode
```

The `tests/test_autogenerated_doccode` directory is intentionally gitignored and should be regenerated locally rather than committed.

## Testing array backends

`Patch` data can be backed by any array library which implements the [array API standard](https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/), so anything written against that standard has to be tested on more than numpy. Fixtures in `tests/test_utils/conftest.py` do this: `backend` is parametrized over every entry in its `BACKENDS` mapping, so a test which asks for it, or for `to_array` or `to_backend`, is collected once per backend without naming any of them.

<!--pytest-codeblocks:skip-->
```python
def test_something(self, random_patch, to_backend, backend):
    """Runs once for every backend in BACKENDS."""
    patch = to_backend(random_patch)         # the same patch, other data
    out = patch.something()
    assert backend_name(out.data) == backend
```

Two backends are tested, and they are chosen because they are the two *kinds* which exist:

- `array_api_strict` implements the standard natively and enforces it pedantically, rejecting anything the specification does not allow. It is what catches numpy assumptions in supposedly portable code.
- `dask` does not implement the standard at all, and is only usable through `array-api-compat`'s wrapper. It is also lazy. Code which recognizes array backends by looking for `__array_namespace__` works for the first kind and silently fails for the second.

Adding another backend is one line in `BACKENDS`. The `pytest.importorskip` lives inside the fixture rather than at the top of the module so that an environment without the test extras skips only the backend tests, rather than the whole file.

Backend tests assert against numpy rather than against hard-coded values. Numpy still runs the original implementation, so the same call on a numpy patch is a live oracle for dtype, dims, coords, attrs, and values.

A patch function which declares `backend="array_api"` must have an entry in `ARRAY_API_CASES` in `tests/test_utils/test_array_api.py`, which says how to exercise it. The test collects every such patch function in dascore and fails if one has no entry, so declaring the array API backend without proving it does not pass CI. That table doubles as the inventory of what has been converted.

## Writing Tests

Tests should go into the `tests/` folder, which mirrors the structure of the main package.
For example, if you are writing tests for `dascore.Patch`, whose class definition is
located in `dascore/core/patch` it should go in `tests/test_core/test_patch.py`.

In general, tests should be grouped together in classes. Fixtures go as close as
possible to the test(s) that need them, moving from class, module, and then to conftest.
Checkout the pytest documentation for a [review on fixtures](https://docs.pytest.org/en/6.2.x/fixture.html)
(and why to use them).
